The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami' al-Bayan) on Surah 26, verse 4:

The interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿If We willed, We could send down upon them from the sky a sign, and their necks would remain humbled before it﴾ [...] The scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding the meaning of His words: ﴿and their necks would remain humbled﴾ ... the verse. Some of them said: its meaning is: the people upon whom a sign would be sent down from the sky would remain, with their necks humbled before it, in abasement.

Mention of those who said that:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿their necks would remain humbled before it﴾, he said: they would remain with their necks humbled before it.

Al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿humbled﴾, he said: If God willed, He would send down upon them a sign by which they would be abased, so that no one would turn his neck toward disobedience to God.

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: (Will they not be believers? If We willed, We could send down upon them from the sky a sign), he said: If God willed, He would show them a matter of His command, after which none of them would act in disobedience.

Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿their necks would remain humbled before it﴾, he said: prostrating their necks.

Yunus narrated to us, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿their necks would remain humbled before it﴾, he said: the khadi' is the abased one.

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: their chiefs and their great men would remain humbled before the sign, and they say: "the necks" means the great men among the people.

The grammarians (ahl al-'Arabiyyah) differed regarding the reason for the masculine form of ﴿khadi'in﴾ (humbled), while it is a predicate referring to ﴿a'naq﴾ (necks). Some grammarians of Basra claimed that His words ﴿a'naquhum﴾ (their necks) are used in the sense of groups, as in: "this is a great neck of people," or it was masculinized as some feminine nouns are masculinized, as the poet said:

"I sipped it while the rooster calls its morning, when the Banu Na'sh drew near and turned about" [a verse recited by Sibawayh for al-Nabigha al-Ja'di (Lisan: n‑'‑sh), preceded by another verse describing wine: "And a pale wine, whose dregs are not hidden, since it is beneath them, is stirred in its vessel, then mixed."]

He said: The Banat Na'sh are seven stars, four of which form a square and three are the daughters (banat) of the bier. The singular is Ibn Na'sh, because the star is masculine, so they masculinize it according to its masculinity. When they say "three" or "four," they refer to the daughters, and likewise the Lesser Banat Na'sh. Sibawayh and al-Farra' agreed on not declining Na'sh because of definiteness and feminine form. It was said that they were likened to the bearers of the bier in their squareness. In poetry, Banu Na'sh also occurs; Sibawayh recited for al-Nabigha al-Ja'di: "And a pale wine..." [the two verses]. Al-Sahba' is wine. His words "whose dregs are not hidden, since it is beneath them" mean that the dregs, if they fall into it, are not concealed by it, because it is clear, so the dregs are seen in it when they fall. His words "since it is beneath them" mean that when the dregs settle at the bottom of the vessel, the observer sees them at the place above which the wine is, and the wine is closer to the observer than the dregs; he means that what is behind it is visible. Tusaffaq means it is passed from vessel to vessel. His words "tamazzaztuha" mean: I drank it little by little. Tuqtab means it is mixed with water. Al-Azhari said: when a poet is compelled, he says "Banu Na'sh," as this poet did, and he recited the verse; the proper wording is "Banat Na'sh," just as they say "Banat Awi" and "Banat 'Irs," the singular being "Ibn 'Irs," and they make feminine the plural of non-human things. The version of Abu 'Ubaydah in (Majaz al-Qur'an, p. 171) is: "I drank when the rooster..." etc., the verse.

And [the poetry] "Banu Na'sh" likewise; and they say "Banat Na'sh" and "Banu Na'sh," and it is said "Banat 'Irs" and "Banu 'Irs." A woman said: "I am a man who does not reveal secrets." He said: a man was mentioned to Ru'bah, and he said: he was one of the "daughters of God's mosques," meaning pebbles.

Some grammarians of Kufa said: this is like the statement of the poet:

"You see their spears hung at their sides, when iron rusts upon the warriors" [a verse cited by Ibn al-Anbari in al-Insaf without attribution; al-Baghdadi likewise did not attribute it in al-Khizanah (2: 411)...]

Its meaning, in his view, is: "their necks remained humbled, they themselves (humbled)," as one says: "your hand, extending it," meaning: "your hand, you extending it," so that the verb is considered as belonging to the first noun and is in fact for the second. Likewise His words: "a woman lamented in her desire for his voice" is really "a woman, you," and the "muhaqqaqah" is the she-camel, except that he connected it to "the man" once it was mentioned.

Another of them said: "al-A'naq" means groups, as one says: "I saw the people gathered toward so-and-so as one neck," so that "al-A'naq" means the groups and the bands. He said: it is also possible that "al-A'naq" means the chiefs and the noble men, so it is as if it were said: "the heads of the people and their great men remained humbled before it." He said: more preferable to me than these two Arabic interpretations is to say: when the necks are humbled, their owners are humbled; so the verb was first attributed to the necks, then "humbled" was attributed to the men, as the poet said:

"Upon a seized hand whose back is… neither the man is shamed nor is he fed" [a verse cited by al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an, fol. 328, where he said regarding His words ﴿their necks remained humbled﴾: the verb belongs to the necks, so one may ask why it did not say "humbled" (feminine). There are several correct answers. First: Mujahid made "al-a'naq" mean the noble men, so "al-a'naq" here is like your saying: "their heads, the heads of the people and their great men, remained humbled." Second: that "al-a'naq" means groups, as you say: "I saw the people gathered toward so-and-so as one neck," making "al-a'naq" mean the groups and bands. The one I prefer among these two linguistic options is that when the necks are humbled, their owners are humbled, so the verb is first attributed to the necks and then "humbled" is attributed to the men, as the poet said "upon a seized hand..." He made the verb feminine because the hand encompasses the back and suffices from it.]

Thus he made the verb of "the back" feminine, because the palm gathers the back and suffices from it, just as you suffice with saying "I submitted to you" rather than "my neck submitted to you." He said: do you not see that the Arabs say "every one who has an eye, a looking one, and looking toward you," because your saying "my eye looked toward you" and "I looked toward you" have one meaning, dropping "every," the verb belonging to the eye and returning to it. So had you said "their necks remained humbled," it would be correct.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: the most correct of these views and the most similar to what the people of interpretation have said is that "the necks" are the necks of the men, and that the meaning of the speech is: "their necks remained abased" before the sign that God sends down upon them from the sky; and that His words "humbled" are masculine because it is a predicate referring to the "ha'" and "mim" in "a'naq," so this is like the verse of Jarir:

"I see the passing of years has taken from me as the crescent takes from the moon" [a verse of Jarir, cited earlier in volume 12, p. 157, and mentioned by the author of Lisan (kh-d-'), who said: it is permissible to predicate of the genitive as the poet said "she saw the passing of the years," since the years cannot be other than what is predicated of the years, though he attributed the passing to them. Al-Sirar is the night in which the crescent is hidden at the end of the month.]

That is because if His words "passing" were removed from the speech, what remained would convey its meaning, and the removal would not corrupt the meaning from what it was before removal; likewise, if "the necks" were removed from His words "their necks remained humbled," what remained would convey its meaning, for when men are abased, their necks are abased, and when their necks are abased, they are abased.

If one were to say, "they remained humbled before it," the speech would not be corrupt by the removal of "the necks," nor would its meaning change from what it was before the removal; so the predicate of humbling is directed to the owners of the necks, even though the speech began with mention of the necks, as is established in the usage of the Arabs when the subject mentioned first and what is attached to it each conveys the predicate of the other.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 26, verses 5–7:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there does not come to them any reminder from the Most Merciful, [but] new, except that they turn away from it.﴾ (5)

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: Those polytheists who deny you and reject what you have brought them, O Muhammad, from your Lord, of admonition and warning concerning the places of God's proofs against them for your truthfulness, and the reality of what you call them to, which God renews for you and reveals to you, so that you may remind them with it, do not come to them except that they turn away from listening to it, and abandon applying their minds to it and reflecting upon it.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they have denied, and there will come to them the news of that at which they used to mock.﴾ (6)

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: So these polytheists have denied, O Muhammad, the reminder that came to them from God, and turned away from it. ﴿So there will come to them the news of that at which they used to mock.﴾ That is: there will come to them the reports of the matter they used to ridicule. This is a threat from God to them that His punishment will descend upon them for their persistence in disbelief and their defiance of their Lord.

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not considered the earth, how many of every noble kind We have caused to grow therein?﴾ (7)

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: Have those polytheists who deny the Resurrection and the raising of the dead not seen the earth, how many [kinds] We have caused to grow therein after it was dead, having no vegetation in it, ﴿of every noble kind﴾? By "noble" (karim) he means "good" (hasan), as one says of a date palm that bears good fruit: "karimah," and of a ewe or a she-camel when they are abundant in milk and their milk is plentiful: "naqah karimah" and "shah karimah."

And the people of interpretation have said in agreement with what we have said concerning its interpretation.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim told us, saying: Isa told us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan told us, saying: Warqa told us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the saying of God: ﴿We caused to grow therein of every noble kind﴾, he said: from the vegetation of the earth, of what people and livestock eat.

- Al-Qasim told us, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

- Al-Hasan told us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: ﴿of every noble kind﴾, he said: good.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 26, verse 8–9:

The exegesis of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed in that is a sign, but most of them would not be believers.﴾ (8) ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful.﴾ (9)

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, in Our causing to grow on the earth every noble pair, there is a sign. That is, a proof for these polytheists who deny the Resurrection of its truth, and that the power by which God caused that vegetation to grow on the earth after its barrenness will not be beyond Him to raise the dead by it after their death, alive from their graves.

* *

As for His words: ﴿But most of them would not be believers﴾

He says: Most of these people who deny the Resurrection, and who reject your prophethood, O Muhammad, were not going to affirm what you bring them from God of the Reminder.

He, may His praise be exalted, says: It has already preceded in My knowledge that they would not believe, so most of them will not believe in you, because of what has preceded in My knowledge concerning them.

* *

As for His words: ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful﴾

He says: And indeed your Lord, O Muhammad, is the Exalted in His retribution, none can resist Him if He wishes to take vengeance upon him. He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Indeed, if I inflict My punishment upon these people who deny you, O Muhammad, who turn away from what comes to them of the Reminder from Me, for their denial of you, no preventer will prevent them from Me, for I am the Exalted in Might, the Merciful, meaning that He is full of mercy toward whoever among His creatures repents from his disbelief and disobedience, so that He does not punish him for the offences he committed before his repentance.

Ibn Jurayj used to say concerning the meaning of this, that:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: al-Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Everything in al-Shu'ara' of His words ﴿the Exalted in Might, the Merciful﴾ refers to what He destroyed of the nations that passed away; He says: Exalted in Might, when He took vengeance upon His enemies, Merciful toward the believers, when He saved them from what He destroyed His enemies with.

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: We chose the view we have chosen here because His words ﴿And indeed, your Lord is the Exalted in Might, the Merciful﴾ come after God's threat to a people of polytheism and the denial of the Resurrection who had not yet been destroyed, so it is not to be directed toward being a report from God about His action against them and His destruction of them. Perhaps Ibn Jurayj, by his saying, meant what occurred after God's report of His destruction of the nations that He destroyed, and that is, God willing, when it follows their report in this way.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 26, verse 10–14:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And when your Lord called out to Moses, "Go to the wrongdoing people, the people of Pharaoh. Will they not fear God?"﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Remember, O Muhammad, when your Lord called out to Moses son of 'Imran, ﴿Go to the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning the disbelievers, the people of Pharaoh. The second "people" is in the accusative as an apposition (tarjamah) to the first "people." His saying, ﴿Will they not fear God?﴾ means: will they not fear God's punishment for their disbelief in Him? The meaning of the speech is: "[Say to] the people of Pharaoh: will they not fear?" The phrase "say to them" is omitted because the context indicates it. It is said "yattaqun" with the yā' and not "tattaqun" with the tā', because the revelation came before the address; had the reading been with the tā', it would have been correct, as in His saying: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: you will be overcome﴾, where it is read "sa-yughlabun" and "sa-tughlabun."

* *

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿He said, "My Lord, I fear that they will deny me, and my breast will be constricted and my tongue will not be eloquent, so send for Aaron. And they have against me a charge of a crime, so I fear that they will kill me."﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: ﴿He said﴾, Moses said to his Lord, ﴿My Lord, I fear﴾ from the people of Pharaoh to whom You commanded me to go, ﴿that they will deny me﴾ when I tell them that You have sent me to them. ﴿And my breast will be constricted﴾ by their denial of me if they deny me. The phrase ﴿and my breast will be constricted﴾ is in the nominative, coordinated with "I fear," and the majority of the readers of the amsar read it with the nominative, meaning: "and indeed my breast is constricted." His saying ﴿and my tongue will not be eloquent﴾ means: and it will not speak the expression of what You send me with to them, because of the impediment that was in his tongue.

* *

His saying: ﴿and my tongue will not be eloquent﴾

It is a clause coordinated with "will be constricted."

* *

His saying: ﴿so send for Aaron﴾

It means Aaron his brother. He did not say "send Aaron to me" so that he might support me and help me, since the meaning of the speech is understood, like the saying of the speaker: "If a calamity befell us, we would turn to you," meaning: "we would turn to you so that you would help us."

* *

His saying: ﴿And they have against me a charge of a crime﴾

It means: the people of Pharaoh have a claim against me of a crime I committed against them, namely his killing of the soul from among them that he killed.

Those who interpret the Qur'an said things similar to what we have said about this.

* *

It means: I fear that they will kill me in retaliation (qawd) for the soul that he killed from among them.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 26, verses 15–17:

The explanation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He said, "No! So go, both of you, with Our signs. Indeed, We are with you, listening.﴾ (15) ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say, 'Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds.'﴾ (16) ﴿[Saying], 'Send with us the Children of Israel.'﴾ (17)

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: ﴿No!﴾ means: the people of Pharaoh will not kill you. ﴿So go, both of you, with Our signs﴾ means: go, you and your brother, with Our signs, that is, with Our proofs and evidences which We have given you against them.

* *

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, We are with you, listening﴾

(means): We hear what the people of Pharaoh say to you and what they answer you with.

* *

And His saying: ﴿So go to Pharaoh and say﴾

... the verse. It means: go, you, O Moses, and your brother Aaron, to Pharaoh. ﴿And say, "Indeed, we are messengers of the Lord of the worlds"﴾ to you, with ﴿Send with us the Children of Israel.﴾ He said "messenger of the Lord of the worlds," and addressed the two with His saying "say" (faqula, in the dual), because He intended by it the verbal noun of "arsalta" (I sent). It is said: "arsaltu risalatan wa rasulan" (I sent a message and a messenger), as the poet said:

*Indeed the slanderers lied; I did not disclose to them anything of ill, nor did I send them as a messenger.* [[The verse is cited in (Lisan al-Arab: rasl). In one narration "bi-Layla" appears in place of "bi-su'". He said: "al-irsal" is directing, and one sends to him. He said: "al-rasul" in the sense of "al-risalah" is feminine and masculine. In (Lisan al-Arab: rasl) there is another narration of the verse like the author's, and he attributes it to Kuthayyir.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 26, verses 18–19:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said: Did we not bring you up among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life? And you did your deed which you did, and you were of the ungrateful.﴾

In this speech there is an ellipsis, dispensed with because of what is indicated by what is manifest from it, and it is: "So they came to Pharaoh and conveyed to him the message of their Lord to him, and Pharaoh said: Did we not bring you up among us as a child, O Musa, and did you not remain among us for years of your life?" That was his stay with him before the killing of the man (qatil) whom he killed from among the Copts. ﴿And you did your deed which you did﴾ means: his killing of the soul which he killed from among the Copts.

Ahl al-ta'wil (the people of interpretation) said things similar to what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said that:

- Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us; and al-Harith related to me, saying: al-Hasan related to us, saying: Warqa' related to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you were of the ungrateful.﴾ He [Musa] said: ﴿I did it then, and I was of the astray.﴾ He said: The killing of the soul.

- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, the like of it.

It was said ﴿And you did your deed﴾ only because it was a single occurrence, and it is not permissible to pronounce the fa' with a kasra when this meaning is intended. It is reported from al-Sha'bi that he recited it: "wa fa'alta fi'latak" with a kasra on the fa', and that is a reading opposed to the readings of the reciters of the metropolitan regions.

* *

As for His words: ﴿and you were of the ungrateful﴾

The people of ta'wil differed in its interpretation. Some of them said: the meaning of that is: "and you were of those who disbelieve in God according to our religion."

Mention of those who said that:

- Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you were of the ungrateful﴾ — meaning: according to this religion of ours which you find fault with.

And others said: rather, the meaning of that is: "and you were of the ungrateful for our favour upon you."

Mention of those who said that:

- Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words: ﴿And you did your deed which you did, and you were of the ungrateful﴾: "We raised you among us as a child; so this is what you have repaid us: you killed a soul from among us, and you denied our favour!"

- Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿and you were of the ungrateful﴾ — he says: "ungrateful for the blessing, because Pharaoh did not know what disbelief (kufr) was."

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This saying which Ibn Zayd stated is more fitting to the interpretation of the verse, because Pharaoh did not acknowledge God's lordship; rather he claimed that he himself was the Lord. It is impermissible that he would say to Musa, if Musa was, in his view, upon his religion on the day he killed the man, as al-Suddi said: "You did the deed and you were of the disbelievers," since faith (iman) in his view is his religion, which Musa was upon in his view — unless a speaker says: he meant: "and you were of the disbelievers on that day, O Musa," according to your saying today, in which case that would be a viable line of interpretation. The meaning of the speech, then, is: "You killed the one whom you killed from among us, and you were of the ungrateful for our favour upon you and our kindness to you in your killing of him."

It has also been said: the meaning of that is: "and you are now of the ungrateful for my favour upon you and my raising you."

**Commentary on the Words of God Most High: ﴿He said, "I did it then, while I was among the misguided" (20). So I fled from you when I feared you, but my Lord granted me judgment and made me among the messengers" (21).﴾**

God, may He be remembered, says: Moses said to Pharaoh, "I committed that deed, namely, I killed that soul which I killed, ﴿then, while I was among the misguided﴾." That is, "I was among the ignorant before revelation from God came to me forbidding his killing." The Arabs use *al-dalal* (misguidance, *ḍalāl*) in place of *al-jahl* (ignorance), and *al-jahl* in place of *al-dalal*. They say, "So-and-so *jahila al-ṭarīq*" and "*ḍalla al-ṭarīq*," meaning the same thing.

Those who engage in *ta'wil* (interpretation of the Qur'an) have said something similar to what we have said.

**Those who said this:**

* Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿and I am among the misguided﴾: "Among the ignorant."

* al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid, the same.

Ibn Juraij said: In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "*wa-anā mina l-jāhilīn*" (وأنا مِنَ الجَاهِلِينَ), "and I am among the ignorant."

* al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Abu Sufyan narrated to us, from Mu'ammar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿and I am among the misguided﴾: "Among the ignorant."

* I was told by al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: Ubayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words ﴿and you are among the disbelievers﴾: Moses said, "I did not disbelieve, but I did it while I was among the misguided." In the variant of Ibn Mas'ud: "*fa-'alartuhā idhan wa-anā mina l-jāhilīn*" (فعلتها إذا وأنا من الجاهلين), "I did it then, while I was among the ignorant."

* Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words ﴿He said, "I did it then, while I was among the misguided"﴾: "Before there came to me anything from God, my killing him was an error, a mistake." He said: "*al-ḍalāla*" here means error, and he did not say *ḍalālah* in what is between him and God.

* Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding ﴿He said, "I did it then, while I was among the misguided"﴾: he means, "while I was among the ignorant."

* * *

As for His words ﴿So I fled from you when I feared you﴾ ... the verse. God, may He be remembered, says, reporting the speech of Moses to Pharaoh: ﴿So I fled from you﴾, O assembly of the chiefs of Pharaoh's people, ﴿when I feared you﴾, that you would kill me in retaliation for the person of yours I had killed. ﴿Then my Lord granted me judgment﴾, meaning: then my Lord granted me prophethood, which is the *ḥukm* (judgment, wisdom).

As:

* Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, regarding ﴿then my Lord granted me judgment﴾: "*al-ḥukm*" is prophethood.

* * *

As for His words ﴿and made me among the messengers﴾:

He means: and He joined me to the company of those whom He sent to His creatures, conveying His message to them by sending me to you, O Pharaoh.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 26, verses 22–24:

Concerning the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And this is a favour with which you reproach me – that you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ (22) ﴿Pharaoh said, "And what is the Lord of the worlds?"﴾ (23) ﴿[Moses] said, "Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, if you should be convinced."﴾ (24)

He, exalted is His remembrance, says, relating the words of His prophet Moses (ﷺ) to Pharaoh: ﴿And this is a favour with which you reproach me﴾. By His saying, "And this" he means Pharaoh's rearing of him, that is: "and your rearing of me, and your leaving off enslaving me, as you enslaved the Children of Israel, is a favour from you with which you reproach me, rightfully." In the speech there is an omitted element, which is dispensed with by the indication of what has been mentioned, namely: "And this is a favour with which you reproach me, that you enslaved the Children of Israel and left me, so you did not enslave me." The mention of "and left me" is omitted because of the indication of His saying ﴿that you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾. The Arabs do this for the sake of brevity in speech. A parallel to this in speech is that two men deserve a punishment from a ruler, so he punishes one of them and pardons the other, and the pardoned man says, "This is a favour upon me from the commander, that he punished so-and-so and left me," and then "and left me" is omitted because the speech indicates it. Also, in His saying ﴿that you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ there are two readings: one is the accusative, since "tamunnuha" is linked to it, and when it is accusative the meaning of the speech is: "And this is a favour with which you reproach me in order that you enslave the Children of Israel." The other is the nominative, on the basis that it is a restatement of "the favour." When it is nominative the meaning of the speech is: "And this is a favour with which you reproach me, your enslaving of the Children of Israel." By His saying ﴿that you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ he means: that you took them as your slaves. It is said from this: "I enslaved the slaves" (ʿabbadtu al-ʿabīd) and "I made them slaves" (aʿbadtuhum). The poet said:

"Why do my people enslave me, when there are many camels in it, and they have whatever they wish, and servants?" [The verse is among the evidences cited in Lisan al-Arab (root ʿ-b-d): one says "taʿabbada al-rajul" and "ʿabbadahu" with doubled bāʾ in both, and "aʿbadahu" means he made him like a slave. The poet said: "Why do my people enslave me…" the verse.]

Those who gave interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said the same as what we have said about this.

Mention of those who said that:

Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqaʾ narrated to us, all of them from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿that you reproach me with it – that you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾: He said: "You subdued them and put them to service."

al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "Reproaching me that you enslaved the Children of Israel": He said: "You subdued, overpowered and employed the Children of Israel."

Musa ibn Harun narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿And this is a favour with which you reproach me – that you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾ and "you reared me before as a child."

Others said: this was a question from Moses to Pharaoh, as if he said: "Do you reproach me that you took the Children of Israel as slaves?"

Mention of those who said that:

al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying ﴿And this is a favour with which you reproach me﴾: He said: Moses says to Pharaoh: "Do you reproach me that you took the Children of Israel as slaves?"

The grammarians (ahl al-ʿarabiyyah) differed on this. Some of the grammarians of Basra said: "And this is a favour with which you reproach me," so it is said: this is a question, as if he said: "Do you reproach me with it?" Then he explained it, saying ﴿that you have enslaved the Children of Israel﴾, and made it a substitute (badal) for "the favour." Some of the grammarians rejected this view and said: it is an error by the one who said it; it is not permissible for the interrogative hamza to be omitted while it is still required, so that the interrogative becomes like a declarative. He said: It has been criticized even when accompanied by "am," which is an indicator of the interrogative, and they criticized:

"Are you departing from the tribe, or are you setting out early? And what harms you if you wait?" [The verse is by Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr al-Kindi (Mukhtar al-Shi'r al-Jahili, ed. Mustafa al-Saqqa, Halabi edition, p. 115). "Tarawwah": "Are you departing"; "tabtakir": leaves early. He says: "Are you going back to your family at the end of the day, or going out to them early in the morning, and what hastens you away from waiting, when it is better for you?" Exalted is He, by His saying ﴿He said to those around him, "Do you not listen?"﴾, it means: Pharaoh said to those around him from his people, "Do you not listen to what Musa says?" He said that and attributed the enemy of Allah, Musa, to madness, because it was his view and the view of his people that there is no lord worthy of worship other than himself, and that what Musa calls them to is falsehood with no reality. So Musa, at that point, argued against them and made known to them their Lord by His attributes and His signs, since for Pharaoh's people the one they recognized as a lord for them at that time was Pharaoh, and what they recognized as lords for their forefathers were other kings who were before Pharaoh and had passed away. The Exegesis of Verse 30–33

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿Moses said: "Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said: "Then bring it, if you are among the truthful."﴾ ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent.﴾ ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white for the onlookers.﴾

His saying, may His remembrance be exalted: Moses said to Pharaoh when his Lord had made him know Him, that He is the Lord of the East and the West, and he called him to worship Him and to devote divinity sincerely to Him. Pharaoh answered him with his words, ﴿"If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among those imprisoned"﴾, meaning: "Will you make me among the imprisoned?" Then [Moses said], ﴿"Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾, which makes clear to you the truthfulness of what I say, O Pharaoh, and the reality of what I call you to. He only said this to him because it is among people's character to yield to fairness and to accept the truth after it has been made clear. So when Moses said to him what he said, Pharaoh said to him: "Then bring the clear thing that shows the reality of what you say, for we will not imprison you then, if you take a god other than me, if you are among the truthful." He means: "If you are right in what you say, and truthful in what you describe and report." ﴿So he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent.﴾ He, may His praise be exalted, says: Moses threw down his staff, and it turned into a serpent (tha'ban), which is the male snake, as I have already explained earlier regarding its description. His saying ﴿clearly visible﴾ means: it made itself clear to Pharaoh and the chiefs of his people that it was a serpent.

The exegetes (ahl al-ta'wil) said things similar to what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said this:

Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Abu Bakr ibn Abd Allah, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words ﴿so he threw down his staff, and behold, it was a clearly visible serpent﴾: it means: clearly showing to him that it created a snake.

His saying ﴿And he drew out his hand, and behold, it was white﴾

He means: Moses drew his hand out from his collar (jayb), and behold, it was white, shining, ﴿for the onlookers﴾, for whoever looked at it and saw it.

Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Uthام ibn Ali narrated to us, saying: al-A'mash narrated to us, from al-Minhal, who said: The serpent rose up into the sky the distance of a mile, then descended until Pharaoh's head was between its two fangs, and it began saying: "O Moses, command me with whatever you wish." Pharaoh began saying: "O Moses, I ask you by the One who sent you." He said: Then its belly seized him.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 26, verses 34–38:

The interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿He said to the eminent ones around him, "Indeed, this is a learned magician.﴾ ﴿He wants to expel you from your land with his magic, so what do you advise?"﴾ ﴿They said, "Postpone him and his brother, and send messengers to the cities to gather [the magicians]﴾ ﴿to bring you every learned magician."﴾

His, the Exalted's, words mean: Pharaoh said, when Moses showed him the great power and authority of God as a proof against him, confirming the truth of what Moses called him to and of what he brought from his Lord, ﴿to the eminent ones around him﴾, meaning the nobles of his people who were around him. ﴿"Indeed, this is a learned magician"﴾ means: Moses has practised magic with his staff until he showed it to you as a serpent. ﴿"Learned"﴾ means: one who has knowledge of magic and expertise in it. ﴿"He wants to expel you from your land with his magic"﴾ means: he wants to bring the Children of Israel out of your land to Syria by overpowering you with magic. He said "he wants to expel you," addressing the eminent ones around him from among the Copts, while the intended people were the Children of Israel, because the Copts had enslaved the Children of Israel and taken them as servants for themselves and as the humiliated. Therefore he said to them, ﴿"He wants to expel you,"﴾ meaning: he wants to expel your servants and slaves from the land of Egypt to Syria.

I have said this is the meaning because God only sent Moses to Pharaoh commanding him to release the Children of Israel with him, so He said to him and to his brother, ﴿"Go to Pharaoh and say, 'We are messengers of the Lord of the worlds, [saying] release the Children of Israel with us.'"﴾

* *

As for His words, ﴿"So what do you advise?"﴾

It means: What do you command concerning the matter of Moses, and what opinion do you point out regarding him? ﴿They said, "Postpone him and his brother, and send messengers to the cities to gather [the magicians]"﴾. His, the Exalted's, words mean: Pharaoh answered the eminent ones around him, and they said to him: Delay Moses and his brother and give them respite, and send to your lands and the cities of Egypt gatherers who will bring to you every learned magician.

**Commentary on the interpretation of His words, the Exalted: "So the sorcerers were assembled for the appointed time of a known day (38). And it was said to the people: 'Will you gather? (39) Perhaps we may follow the sorcerers if they are the victors' (40)."**

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: The gatherers whom Pharaoh sent assembled the sorcerers "for the appointed time of a known day," meaning: for a time that Pharaoh had promised Moses, that they would meet with him at it, on a known day, and that was the Day of Adornment, "and that the people be gathered in the forenoon."

"And it was said to the people: will you gather together," in order to watch what the two parties do, and to whom victory will go, to Moses or to the sorcerers? "Perhaps we may follow the sorcerers": the meaning of "perhaps" (la'alla) here is "so that." He says: so that we may follow the sorcerers, "if they are the victors" over Moses. I have said this to clarify its meaning: because the people of Pharaoh were upon the religion of Pharaoh, it is not reasonable for one who holds a religion to say, "Look at the proof of the one who opposes me, perhaps I will follow my religion"; rather, one says, "Look at it so that I may increase in insight into my religion, and so I may establish it." Thus the people of Pharaoh spoke. It is this that they intended by their saying: "Perhaps we may follow the sorcerers if they are the victors."

And it has been said: their gathering for the appointed time at which Pharaoh and Moses had agreed to meet was at Alexandria.

Mention of those who said that:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words, "And it was said to the people: will you gather together?" He said: They were at Alexandria. Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 26, verses 45–50:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Moses threw down his staff, and behold, it swallowed up what they were falsely showing.﴾ ﴿So the sorcerers fell down prostrating.﴾ ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Have you believed in Him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. But you are going to know. I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will surely crucify you all."﴾

His exalted remembrance says: ﴿Then Moses threw down his staff﴾ when the sorcerers threw their ropes and their staffs. ﴿And behold, it swallowed up what they were falsely showing﴾ meaning: behold, the staff of Moses swallowed what they were bringing of falsehood and magic that has no reality, and which was nothing but imaginings (makhayil [[makhayil: the plural of makhayila, meaning a suspicion or appearance; its root is makhayil. The Kufans add a yā' before the last letter in plurals of this type, as in dārāhim and ṣayārif, the plurals of dirham and ṣayraf.]]) and deception. ﴿Then the sorcerers fell down prostrating﴾ meaning: when the sorcerers realized that what Moses had brought them was truth and not magic, and that it is something that none can do except God, who originated the heavens and the earth without precedent, they fell prostrate upon their faces in adoration of God, submitting to Him in obedience, acknowledging to Moses that what he had brought them from God is the truth, and that what they had been doing of magic is false, saying: ﴿We have believed in the Lord of the worlds﴾ who was called upon by Moses to be worshipped instead of Pharaoh and his chiefs. ﴿The Lord of Moses and Aaron.﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Have you believed in Him before I give you permission?"﴾ His exalted remembrance says: Pharaoh said to those who had been his sorcerers and then believed: Have you believed in Moses, that what he brought is true, before I gave you permission to believe in him? ﴿Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic﴾ meaning: indeed Moses is your leader in magic, and it is he who taught you it, and that is why you believed in him. ﴿But you are going to know﴾ at the time of my punishment of you, the consequence of what you did and the error of what you did in believing in him.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿They said, "No harm. Indeed, we are to our Lord returning."﴾

His saying ﴿I will surely cut off your hands and your feet﴾ means: differing in the cutting of that among you, between cutting the hands and the feet; that is, I will cut the right hand and the left foot, then the left hand and the right foot, and so on, cutting a hand from one side and the foot from the other side, and that is cutting from opposite sides. ﴿And I will surely crucify you all﴾ he emphasized this with "all," informing them that he would spare none of them. ﴿They said, "No harm"﴾ His exalted remembrance says: The sorcerers said: No harm upon us. It is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "So-and-so has harmed so-and-so, so he harms him, harm," and its meaning is: no harm.

And those who interpret the Qur'an have said the like of what we have said about this.

Those who said so:

Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning His saying: ﴿No harm﴾ he said: It means: what you say does not harm us, even if you do it to us and crucify us. ﴿Indeed, we are to our Lord returning﴾ meaning: indeed we are returning to our Lord, and He will reward us for our patience under your punishment of us, and our steadfastness in His monotheism and our disavowal of disbelief in Him.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 26, verses 53–56:

The interpretation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿So Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers (ḥāshirīn). ﴾ ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band (shirdhimah qalīlūn).﴾ ﴿And indeed, they have enraged us (la-ghāʾiẓūn).﴾ ﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant (ḥādhirūn) multitude.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Pharaoh sent into the cities to gather for him his troops and his people, and said to them: ﴿Indeed, these﴾ — by "these" he means the Children of Israel — ﴿are but a small band (shirdhimah qalīlūn)﴾. By "shirdhimah" is meant a group and a remnant, the remaining small portion of a troop (ʿuṣbah) of Jubayrah; and the shirdhimah of anything is its small remaining part. From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"The winter has come, and my shirt is worn out... / tatters (sharādhim) at which the ṭawwāq laughs."

[[The verse is cited in (Lisan al-ʿArab: kh-l-q) as attributed to a rajaz poet. He said: it is said "thawb akhlāq" (a worn garment), they describe the singular with it when the wear is in all of it, just as they said "burmah aʿshār" (a pot in pieces) and "ḥabl armām" (a rope in pieces) and "arḍ sabāsib"; and likewise "burmah akhlāq" according to al-Liḥyānī, meaning its sides are worn. And the rajaz poet said: "The winter has come..." the verse. End. It is as if, since it had become entirely worn, every part of it was worn, so he pluralised it according to its parts, as al-Liḥyānī's expression indicates. Al-Tawwāq: the name of the rajaz poet's son. And in (Lisan al-ʿArab: sh-r-dh-m) the shirdhimah: a piece of a thing, its plural is sharādhim; and the shirdhimah is a small group of people; and in the revelation: "Indeed, these are but a small band (shirdhimah) qalīlūn"; and "thiyāb sharādhim" means torn worn-out garments, and "thawb sharādhim" means pieces. And he cited the verse from Ibn Burrī.]]

It is also said: "qalīlūn" (plural), because each group among them carried the meaning of paucity; when he gathered them, he used the plural for their groups, as al-Kumayt said:

"He turned back the outlying tribes of them, so they have become like one tribe we are."

[[The verse is by al-Kumayt (Lisan al-ʿArab: w-ḥ-d). Al-Jawhari said: the Arabs say "antum ḥayy wāḥid" and "ḥayy wāḥidūn," as one says "shirdhimah qalīlūn," and he cited for al-Kumayt: "He turned back the outlying tribes..." the verse. It resembles the words of al-Farrāʾ in his Maʿānī al-Qurʾān (the Jamiʿah manuscript, folio 229): he said: "His saying: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band, qalīlūn﴾ means: a small troop, and qalīlūn and kathīrūn. Most of the Arabs' speech is that they say: 'your people is few (qalīl) and our people is many (kathīr).' Qalīlūn and kathīrūn is permissible Arabic; it is permissible because paucity applies to all of them together, so it was said qalīl; and qalīl was preferred over qalīlīn, and the plural is permitted when paucity applies to all of them in meaning, so their names appear accordingly. Similar is 'you are one tribe (ḥayy wāḥid)' and 'ḥayy wāḥidūn.' The meaning of wāḥidūn is wāḥid, as al-Kumayt said: 'He turned back the outlying tribes...' the verse."]]

It is mentioned that the group which Pharaoh called a small band were six hundred and seventy thousand.

Mention of those who said so:

- Ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told us, saying: Sufyān told us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Abū ʿUbaydah: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾, he said: they were six hundred and seventy thousand.

- He said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told us, saying: Isrāʾīl told us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Abū ʿUbaydah, from ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd), he said: the shirdhimah: six hundred thousand and seventy thousand.

- Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Wāḍiḥ told us, saying: Mūsā ibn ʿUbaydah told us, from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaddād ibn al-Hād, he said: Yaʿqūb and his offspring, who were seventy-two, gathered to Yūsuf; and they went out with Mūsā, and they were six hundred thousand. Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾, and Pharaoh went out on a dark, stallion horse of the colour of his horse in his army, eight hundred thousand.

- Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, saying: Ibn ʿUlayyah told us, from Saʿīd al-Jurayrī, from Abū al-Sulayl, from Qays ibn ʿAbbād, he said: and he was among the people who most or most recently narrated about the Children of Israel. He said: he told us that the shirdhimah whom Pharaoh named from the Children of Israel were six hundred thousand. He said: the vanguard of Pharaoh was seven hundred thousand, each man of them on a horse with a helmet on his head and a spear in his hand, and he was behind them in the dahm (the mass). When Mūsā brought the Children of Israel to the sea, the Children of Israel said: O Mūsā, where is what you promised us? This sea is before us, and this is Pharaoh and his troops who have overtaken us from behind. Mūsā said to the sea: "Split, Abū Khālid." He said: "No, I will not split for you, O Mūsā; I am older than you in creation." He said: it was proclaimed: "Strike the sea with your staff," and he struck it, and the sea split, and they were twelve tribes. Al-Jurayrī said: I think he said that each tribe had a path. He said: when the first of Pharaoh's troops reached the sea, the horses shied away from the sea; he said: a mare was displayed from them, and it smelt her scent and was roused, so the horses followed it. He said: when the last of Pharaoh's troops had entered the sea and the last of the Children of Israel had come out, He commanded the sea, and it closed over them. The Children of Israel said: Pharaoh has not died, and he would never die. God heard their denial, so He sent to His Prophet, peace be upon him, he said: He cast him onto the shore, like a red bull which the Children of Israel viewed.

- Mūsā narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr told us, saying: Asbāṭ told us, from al-Suddī, concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾: meaning the Children of Israel.

- Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim told us, saying: ʿĪsā told us; and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥasan told us, saying: Warqāʾ told us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾: he said: they on that day were six hundred thousand, and the number of Pharaoh's companions cannot be counted.

- Al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn told us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Mūsā: Travel by night with My servants, indeed you will be pursued﴾. He said: God revealed to Mūsā that he should gather the Children of Israel, every four households in one house, then slaughter lambs and strike their blood upon the doors, for I will command the angels not to enter a house whose door has blood. And I will command them to kill the firstborn of Pharaoh's family, from among themselves and their wealth. Then bake unleavened bread, for it is quicker for you. Then travel by night with My servants until you reach the sea, and My command will come to you. He did so. When they awoke, Pharaoh said: this is the work of Mūsā and his people; they have killed our firstborn from among ourselves and our wealth. So he sent in pursuit of them one million and five hundred thousand and five hundred kings equipped, with each king a thousand men, and Pharaoh went out in the great army, and said ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾. He said: a fragment; and they were six hundred thousand, two hundred thousand of them being from twenty to forty years old.

- He said: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Abū Bakr ibn Ḥawshab, from Ibn ʿAbbās, he said: with Pharaoh that day was a thousand tyrants, all of them wearing a crown, and all of them commanders over horses.

- He said: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, he said: there were thirty kings as a rearguard behind Pharaoh, thinking they were with them, and Jibrīl was in front of them, turning the front of the horses back upon their rear; and he followed them until he reached the sea. As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, they have enraged us﴾, it means: indeed these small band have enraged us. He mentioned that their enragement at them was the killing of the angels of those of their firstborn who were killed.

Mention of those who said so:

- Al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn told us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying: ﴿And indeed, they have enraged us﴾, meaning: by their killing our firstborn from among ourselves and our wealth. It may also be that its meaning is: they have enraged us by their departure with what they had borrowed from us of the ornaments, and it may be by their separation from them and their leaving our land against our will.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant multitude (ḥādhirūn)﴾

The readers differed in reciting this. The majority of the Kufan readers recited ﴿ḥādhirūn﴾, meaning: they are prepared, equipped, possessors of instruments, strength and weapons. The majority of the readers of Madinah and Basra recited "wa-anā la-jamīʿun ḥadhirūn" without the alif. Al-Farrāʾ used to say: it is as if the ḥādhir is the one who is now wary of you, and as if the ḥadhar (wariness) is created as wariness, you do not meet it except wary; and from ḥadhar is the saying of Ibn Aḥmar:

"Shall you postpone a day to another? / Indeed I am ḥawālī (shrewd), and I am ḥadhir (wary)."

[[The verse is by Ibn Aḥmar al-Bāhilī. The author said so. In (Lisan al-ʿArab: ḥ-w-l) it is attributed to al-Marrār ibn Munqidh al-ʿAdawī. He said: it is said a man is ḥawālī: for one of sound opinion and resource, as Ibn Aḥmar said; it is said of al-Marrār ibn Munqidh al-ʿAdawī: "Or will you postpone my day to another?"

And he said under "ḥ-dh-r": a man is ḥadhir and ḥadhar (with the dhāl vowelled with kasra and damma), and ḥādhūrah, and ḥadhiryān: alert, very wary, fearful, cautious. Ḥādhir: prepared, equipped, as if he is wary of being surprised. The plural is ḥadhirūn and ḥidhārā. In the revelation: "And indeed we are a vigilant multitude (ḥādhirūn)", and ḥadhirūn and ḥadhirūn were read; the latter with dammah on the dhāl, reported by al-Akhfash. The meaning of ḥādhirūn is prepared, and the meaning of ḥadhirūn is fearful. It was said: the meaning of ḥadhirūn is equipped. Al-Azharī: whoever reads "wa-innā la-jamīʿun ḥādhirūn" means prepared. He said: he told us that the shirdhimah whom Pharaoh named from the Children of Israel were six hundred thousand. He said: the vanguard of Pharaoh was seven hundred thousand, each man of them on a horse with a helmet on his head and a spear in his hand, and he was behind them in the dahm (the mass). Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 26, verses 53–56:

The interpretation of the words of the Exalted: ﴿So Pharaoh sent into the cities gatherers (ḥāshirīn). ﴾ ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band (shirdhimah qalīlūn).﴾ ﴿And indeed, they have enraged us (la-ghāʾiẓūn).﴾ ﴿And indeed, we are a vigilant (ḥādhirūn) multitude.﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Pharaoh sent into the cities to gather for him his troops and his people, and said to them: ﴿Indeed, these﴾ — by "these" he means the Children of Israel — ﴿are but a small band (shirdhimah qalīlūn)﴾. By "shirdhimah" is meant a group and a remnant, the remaining small portion of a troop (ʿuṣbah) of Jubayrah; and the shirdhimah of anything is its small remaining part. From this is the saying of the rajaz poet:

"The winter has come, and my shirt is worn out... / tatters (sharādhim) at which the ṭawwāq laughs."

[[The verse is cited in (Lisan al-ʿArab: kh-l-q) as attributed to a rajaz poet. He said: it is said "thawb akhlāq" (a worn garment), they describe the singular with it when the wear is in all of it, just as they said "burmah aʿshār" (a pot in pieces) and "ḥabl armām" (a rope in pieces) and "arḍ sabāsib"; and likewise "burmah akhlāq" according to al-Liḥyānī, meaning its sides are worn. And the rajaz poet said: "The winter has come..." the verse. End. It is as if, since it had become entirely worn, every part of it was worn, so he pluralised it according to its parts, as al-Liḥyānī's expression indicates. Al-Tawwāq: the name of the rajaz poet's son. And in (Lisan al-ʿArab: sh-r-dh-m) the shirdhimah: a piece of a thing, its plural is sharādhim; and the shirdhimah is a small group of people; and in the revelation: "Indeed, these are but a small band (shirdhimah) qalīlūn"; and "thiyāb sharādhim" means torn worn-out garments, and "thawb sharādhim" means pieces. And he cited the verse from Ibn Burrī.]]

It is also said: "qalīlūn" (plural), because each group among them carried the meaning of paucity; when he gathered them, he used the plural for their groups, as al-Kumayt said:

"He turned back the outlying tribes of them, so they have become like one tribe we are."

[[The verse is by al-Kumayt (Lisan al-ʿArab: w-ḥ-d). Al-Jawhari said: the Arabs say "antum ḥayy wāḥid" and "ḥayy wāḥidūn," as one says "shirdhimah qalīlūn," and he cited for al-Kumayt: "He turned back the outlying tribes..." the verse. It resembles the words of al-Farrāʾ in his Maʿānī al-Qurʾān (the Jamiʿah manuscript, folio 229): he said: "His saying: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band, qalīlūn﴾ means: a small troop, and qalīlūn and kathīrūn. Most of the Arabs' speech is that they say: 'your people is few (qalīl) and our people is many (kathīr).' Qalīlūn and kathīrūn is permissible Arabic; it is permissible because paucity applies to all of them together, so it was said qalīl; and qalīl was preferred over qalīlīn, and the plural is permitted when paucity applies to all of them in meaning, so their names appear accordingly. Similar is 'you are one tribe (ḥayy wāḥid)' and 'ḥayy wāḥidūn.' The meaning of wāḥidūn is wāḥid, as al-Kumayt said: 'He turned back the outlying tribes...' the verse."]]

It is mentioned that the group which Pharaoh called a small band were six hundred and seventy thousand.

Mention of those who said so:

- Ibn Bashshār narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told us, saying: Sufyān told us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Abū ʿUbaydah: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾, he said: they were six hundred and seventy thousand.

- He said: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān told us, saying: Isrāʾīl told us, from Abū Isḥāq, from Abū ʿUbaydah, from ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd), he said: the shirdhimah: six hundred thousand and seventy thousand.

- Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Yaḥyā ibn Wāḍiḥ told us, saying: Mūsā ibn ʿUbaydah told us, from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazī, from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Shaddād ibn al-Hād, he said: Yaʿqūb and his offspring, who were seventy-two, gathered to Yūsuf; and they went out with Mūsā, and they were six hundred thousand. Pharaoh said: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾, and Pharaoh went out on a dark, stallion horse of the colour of his horse in his army, eight hundred thousand.

- Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to me, saying: Ibn ʿUlayyah told us, from Saʿīd al-Jurayrī, from Abū al-Sulayl, from Qays ibn ʿAbbād, he said: and he was among the people who most or most recently narrated about the Children of Israel. He said: he told us that the shirdhimah whom Pharaoh named from the Children of Israel were six hundred thousand. He said: the vanguard of Pharaoh was seven hundred thousand, each man of them on a horse with a helmet on his head and a spear in his hand, and he was behind them in the dahm (the mass). When Mūsā brought the Children of Israel to the sea, the Children of Israel said: O Mūsā, where is what you promised us? This sea is before us, and this is Pharaoh and his troops who have overtaken us from behind. Mūsā said to the sea: "Split, Abū Khālid." He said: "No, I will not split for you, O Mūsā; I am older than you in creation." He said: it was proclaimed: "Strike the sea with your staff," and he struck it, and the sea split, and they were twelve tribes. Al-Jurayrī said: I think he said that each tribe had a path. He said: when the first of Pharaoh's troops reached the sea, the horses shied away from the sea; he said: a mare was displayed from them, and it smelt her scent and was roused, so the horses followed it. He said: when the last of Pharaoh's troops had entered the sea and the last of the Children of Israel had come out, He commanded the sea, and it closed over them. The Children of Israel said: Pharaoh has not died, and he would never die. God heard their denial, so He sent to His Prophet, peace be upon him, he said: He cast him onto the shore, like a red bull which the Children of Israel viewed.

- Mūsā narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr told us, saying: Asbāṭ told us, from al-Suddī, concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾: meaning the Children of Israel.

- Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim told us, saying: ʿĪsā told us; and al-Ḥārith narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥasan told us, saying: Warqāʾ told us, all of them from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾: he said: they on that day were six hundred thousand, and the number of Pharaoh's companions cannot be counted.

- Al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn told us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying: ﴿And We revealed to Mūsā: Travel by night with My servants, indeed you will be pursued﴾. He said: God revealed to Mūsā that he should gather the Children of Israel, every four households in one house, then slaughter lambs and strike their blood upon the doors, for I will command the angels not to enter a house whose door has blood. And I will command them to kill the firstborn of Pharaoh's family, from among themselves and their wealth. Then bake unleavened bread, for it is quicker for you. Then travel by night with My servants until you reach the sea, and My command will come to you. He did so. When they awoke, Pharaoh said: this is the work of Mūsā and his people; they have killed our firstborn from among ourselves and our wealth. So he sent in pursuit of them one million and five hundred thousand and five hundred kings equipped, with each king a thousand men, and Pharaoh went out in the great army, and said ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾. He said: a fragment; and they were six hundred thousand, two hundred thousand of them being from twenty to forty years old.

- He said: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Abū Bakr ibn Ḥawshab, from Ibn ʿAbbās, he said: with Pharaoh that day was a thousand tyrants, all of them wearing a crown, and all of them commanders over horses.

- He said: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, he said: there were thirty kings as a rearguard behind Pharaoh, thinking they were with them, and Jibrīl was in front of them, turning the front of the horses back upon their rear; and he followed them until he reached the sea. As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, they have enraged us﴾, it means: indeed these small band have enraged us. He mentioned that their enragement at them was the killing of the angels of those of their firstborn who were killed.

Mention of those who said so:

- Al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn told us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying: ﴿And indeed, they have enraged us﴾, meaning: by their killing our firstborn from among ourselves and our wealth. It may also be that its meaning is: they have enraged us by their departure with what they had borrowed from us of the ornaments, and it may be by their separation from them and their leaving our land against our will.

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So We expelled them from gardens and springs (57), and treasures and a noble station (58). Thus, and We bequeathed them to the Children of Israel (59). So they pursued them at sunrise (60).﴾

He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: So We expelled Pharaoh and his people from gardens of water-springs, and treasures of gold and silver, and a noble station. It has been said: that noble station means the pulpits.

* *

That is, in this manner We expelled them from that, as I have described to you in this verse and the one before it. ﴿And We bequeathed them﴾ means: And We bequeathed those gardens from which We expelled them, and the springs, treasures and noble station, to the Children of Israel, by destroying them.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾

Pharaoh and his companions followed the Children of Israel, at sunrise, when the sun had risen; and it has been said, when they had entered the morning.

⁕ Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾, he said: Musa went out by night, and the moon eclipsed and the earth grew dark. His companions said: Yusuf informed us that we would be delivered from Pharaoh, and he took a covenant from us that we would surely depart with his bones with us. She brought it out for him by her wisdom (and her wisdom, or a word resembling this, was that she said): "Carry me and take me out with you." So he placed the bones of Yusuf in his cloak, then carried the old woman on his cloak and placed her upon his neck. And the horses of Pharaoh, filling their bridles, appeared to them as running swiftly (in their eyes), yet they did not move; they were held back from Musa and his companions until they had gone out of sight.

⁕ Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, saying: Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Hasan narrated to us, saying: Warqa narrated to us, all of them, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding ﴿So they pursued them at sunrise﴾, he said: Musa went out by night, and the moon eclipsed and the earth grew dark. His companions said: Yusuf informed us that we would be delivered from Pharaoh, and he took a covenant from us that we would surely depart with his bones with us. So Musa went out that night seeking his grave, and he found an old woman whose house was built over his grave. She brought it out for him by her wisdom (and her wisdom, or a word resembling this, was that she said): "Carry me and take me out with you." So he placed the bones of Yusuf in his cloak, then carried the old woman on his cloak and placed her upon his neck. And the horses of Pharaoh, filling their bridles, appeared to them as running swiftly (in their eyes), yet they did not move; they were held back from Musa and his companions until they had gone out of sight.

* *

As related:

⁕ Ibn Humayd related to me, saying: Salama related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, from ʿAbd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadi, who said: It has been mentioned to me that Pharaoh set out in pursuit of Moses with seventy thousand dark-coloured horses, besides what was in his army of horses of various colours, and Moses went out until the sea confronted him and there was no turning back; Pharaoh appeared with his army behind them. ﴿When the two hosts saw each other, the companions of Moses said, "Indeed, we are overtaken." He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ — meaning, to salvation, and He has promised me that, and there is no breaking of His promise.

⁕ Musa related to us, saying: ʿAmr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿He said, "No! Indeed, with me is my Lord; He will guide me."﴾ — he means: "He will suffice me." And He said: ﴿It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy and make you successors in the land, and see how you will act﴾. As for His words: ﴿Then We inspired to Moses, "Strike with your staff the sea," and it parted﴾, it is mentioned that Allah had commanded the sea not to part until Moses struck it with his staff.

⁕ Musa related to us, saying: ʿAmr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: Then Aaron advanced and struck the sea, but it refused to open, and said: "Who is this tyrant who strikes me?" Then Moses came to it and addressed it by the kunya Abu Khalid, and struck it, and it parted.

⁕ Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, saying: Allah inspired to the sea, as it is mentioned: "When Moses strikes you with his staff, part for him." So the sea began to strike itself against itself out of fear of Allah and awaiting His command. Allah inspired to Moses: "Strike the sea with your staff," so he struck it with it, and in it was the authority of Allah which He had given him, and it parted.

⁕ Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abu Ahmad related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us — Sulayman al-Taymi thought — from Abu al-Sulayl, who said: When Moses struck the sea with his staff, he said: "Ayha, Abu Khalid," and he was seized with a shiver (afkal).

⁕ al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, and Hajjaj from Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah and others, who said: When Moses reached the sea and the wind rose, and the sea was throwing up its current and surging like mountains, and Allah had inspired to the sea not to part until Moses struck it with the staff, Yushaʿ said to him: "O Kalim Allah, where were you commanded?" He said: "Here." He said: So it passed over the sea, the water not covering its hoof. The people set about doing the same, but they could not. The man who concealed his faith said to him: "O Kalim Allah, where were you commanded?" He said: "Here." So he reined in his horse with its bridle until the foam flew from its jaws; then he plunged it into the sea and it sank in the water. Then Allah inspired to Moses: "Strike the sea with your staff," so Moses struck the sea with his staff and it parted, and behold, the man was standing on his horse, his saddle and its covering not wetted.

* *

His words: ﴿And each part was like a great mountain.﴾

He, may He be exalted and remembered, says: each division of the sea, when Moses struck it, was like a great mountain. It is mentioned that it parted into twelve pieces, according to the number of the tribes, with each tribe having a part.

Those of the interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said what we have said regarding this.

Mention of those who said this:

⁕ Musa related to us, saying: ʿAmr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿So it parted, and each part was like a great mountain﴾ — he said: like a great mountain. So the Children of Israel entered, and in the sea there were twelve paths, in each path a tribe. The path was like walls that had split apart. Each tribe said: "Our companions have been killed." When Moses saw that, he called upon Allah, and He made them into arches like vaulted passages, so the last of them could see the first until they all came out.

⁕ al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, and Hajjaj from Abu Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah and others, who said: The sea split, and each part was like a great mountain: twelve paths, in each path a tribe, and the Children of Israel were twelve tribes, and the paths were with walls. Each tribe said: "Our companions have been killed." When Moses saw that, he called upon Allah, and He made them into arches like vaulted passages, so they looked at one another, and on dry land as though the water had never touched it, until they crossed.

He said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: When the sea split for them, there became in it openings through which they could see one another.

⁕ Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me: ﴿And each part was like a great mountain﴾ — that is, like a mountain on a rise of land.

⁕ ʿAli related to me, saying: Muʿawiya related to me, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas, regarding His words: ﴿And each part was like a great mountain﴾ — he said: like a mountain.

⁕ It was reported from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: ʿUbayd informed us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak say, concerning His words: ﴿like a great mountain﴾: "like a great mountain."

And from it is the saying of al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur:

They camped at Anqara, over them flows the water of the Euphrates, coming from the mountains (aṭwād)[[The verse is by al-Aswad ibn Yaʿfur, cited by the author. It is among the witnesses of Abu ʿUbayda in Majaz al-Quran (Jami'a manuscript, p. 172), who said: "like a great mountain": that is, a mountain. He said: "They camped at Anqara..." the verse. In Lisan al-ʿArab (ṭ-w-d): al-ṭawd: a great mountain. In the hadith of ʿA'isha describing her father (may Allah be pleased with them both): "That is a lofty ṭawd," meaning a high mountain. Al-ṭawd: a hill, according to Ibn al-Aʿrabi. Its plural is aṭwād. Ends. In Abu ʿUbayda's narration in Majaz al-Quran the word is "yajish" in place of "yasil". Al-Bakri's narration in Mu'jam ma ista'jam p. 204 (Cairo edition) reads "yasil" as in the author's narration. Anqara is a place on the back of Kufa, below al-Khawarnaq, where Iyad used to dwell in ancient times when they prevailed over what lay between Kufa and Basra. Al-Bakri said: today Tayy and Sulayh live there, and in Bariq toward Hayth and what adjoins it, all dwellings of Tayy and Sulayh. This is the saying of ʿUmar ibn Shabba. Others said: Anqara is a place in al-Hira. They have clarified that this Anqara is other than the Anqara in the lands of Rome (Anatolia), which is now the capital of the Turkish state.]]

By aṭwād is meant the plural of ṭawd, which is the mountain.
